title: sandhi plainly
hook: a king loses to a sage, wants the sage's title, and the title turns out to be two words joined
tomorrow: if a long a can hide a short one, how would anyone know?

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandhi plainly ended a week with the padapatha: a verse chanted with every join undone, then joined again. Today a join hides inside a title, and a king who wanted it badly.

The king has just lost, and he can't believe it. He rode into a forest hermitage with an army, wanting one thing the sage Vasishtha had: a cow that could give whatever was asked of her. Vasishtha wouldn't part with her. The army couldn't take her. So King Vishvamitra sets down his bow and makes a new plan. If a seer beat him, he'll become a seer. He leaves the throne for long, hard austerity, and in the Ramayana's telling, the god Brahma finally comes to him with a title. The king hears it, and he's furious.
screen: `A KING LOSES TO A SAGE.` → `HE LEAVES THE THRONE.` → `A TITLE, AND HE'S FURIOUS.`

segments.voice: The title was rajarshi: a royal seer, a king who is also a sage. To most ears, an honor. To Vishvamitra, a ceiling. A king who had become a seer was still, in that name, a king first. He wanted brahmarshi, the title of a brahmin seer, the one Vasishtha held. So he goes back to his austerities, and the story walks him up a ladder of names, through maharshi, great seer, until at last he's called brahmarshi, and Vasishtha himself greets him by it. Now listen to those names, because each one is a join. Raja and rishi. Maha and rishi. Brahma and rishi. Each time, a word ending in a meets the vowel ri, and the two become ar. Rajarshi. Maharshi. Brahmarshi. It's the same rule that put the e in Ganesha. Panini writes it in two words, ad gunah: after a, the strengthened vowel. For i, that's e. For u, it's o. For ri, it's ar. So when an ar turns up in the middle of a long word, it's a door worth trying. Could this be an a and a ri? The title Vishvamitra fought for turns out to be two plain words, leaning together. And tradition gives him one more thing to be remembered by: it names him the seer of the Gayatri.
screen: `RAJARSHI: A ROYAL SEER.` · `UP THE LADDER TO BRAHMARSHI.` · `A AND RI BECOME AR.` · `AN AR CAN BE A DOOR.` · then, large: `TWO PLAIN WORDS, JOINED.`

segments.voice: Say the three pairs out loud, slowly, apart and then joined: raja, rishi, rajarshi; maha, rishi, maharshi; brahma, rishi, brahmarshi. Feel the a and the ri fold into ar on the tongue. Then let the names go quiet, and sit with the breath.
Sandhi plainly: where words meet, and their sounds give way to each other. Today, an a and a ri becoming ar, in the titles of seers.
Keep this one: sandhi plainly, and a seer's title can be two words joined. Day done.

howItsDone: Students of Sanskrit learn sandhi by splitting compounds back into their words; titles such as rishi, maharshi and rajarshi are used for revered seers, and the Gayatri is recited at dawn by those who keep it.

fork.setup: a baby cousin is named Devarshi. at the naming, an aunt asks what's inside the name. what do you say?
options: deva and rishi: a god and a seer, the a and ri joined as ar.
devar and shi: two old words, brother-in-law and peace.
nothing inside: it's one old name with no parts.
fork.reveal: the same join as rajarshi and maharshi: a word ending in a meets ri, and they become ar. deva plus rishi, a divine seer.

original.note: Sanskrit: a royal seer, from raja, king, and rishi, seer; a and ri join as ar.

trapdoor: what you thought: maharshi is just a fancy word for a holy man.
what it means: maha, great, plus rishi, seer; the a and the ri join as ar.
what a scholar hears: guna sandhi, Panini's ad gunah, with ri strengthened to ar; the same rule that gives e and o.
recall: namah + te: the h turns to s
gana + isha: a and i make e

chat.says: essay prompt: 'something you inherited.' found nani's old gita. she penciled 'maha + rishi' over maharshi. bad speller??
options: no, she was undoing a join: a meets ri and becomes ar, so it's maha plus rishi.
probably: maharshi is one old word, and the plus sign was her own guess.
she was fixing a typo: the printer dropped an i, so it should read maharishi.
chat.meaning: In sandhi, a before ri becomes ar: maha plus rishi gives maharshi. Nani's pencil was taking the join apart.

Vishvamitra.meaning: a king who became a seer; tradition names him the Gayatri's seer

Vasishtha.meaning: a sage whose wish-granting cow the king tried to take

rajarshi.meaning: a royal seer: raja, king, plus rishi, seer

brahmarshi.meaning: a brahmin seer: brahma plus rishi

Gayatri.meaning: a Rig Veda verse recited at dawn

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda (the story of Vishvamitra and Vasishtha: the cow, the austerities, the titles rajarshi, maharshi, brahmarshi)

Rig Veda 3.62.10 (the Gayatri), credited by tradition to Vishvamitra

notes: 2026-10-14 v3 rewrite (recipe v3): story shape. Rewritten from the older draft, which took the -ah to -o join through the Gayatri; that rule now lives on day 1461 (atithidevo bhava), and the Gayatri is only named, not chanted, since some communities keep it for the initiated. This day keeps the title, word, carry and the Rig Veda 3.62.10 citation. Priya's two-week storyline starts here: her college essay about something inherited, Nani's pencil-marked Gita.

Ramayana check: the sequence of titles (rajarshi, then rishi, then maharshi, then brahmarshi, with Vasishtha acknowledging him) follows the Bala Kanda chapters on Vishvamitra; the lesson names rajarshi, maharshi and brahmarshi only. Confirm wording 'Vasishtha himself greets him by it'. The violent parts of the story (the sons) are left out on purpose.
Grammar: a + ri = ar under ad gunah (6.1.87) with uran raparah (1.1.51). Devarshi in the fork = deva + rishi; confirm.
'Tradition names him the seer of the Gayatri': the third mandala of the Rig Veda is ascribed to Vishvamitra's family; kept as tradition, not fact.
